settings.heading: They Wake Up With a Dry Mouth
settings.subheading: Does your child immediately reach for water in the morning?
settings.body:
Sleeping with the mouth open can leave the mouth and throat feeling noticeably dry by morning.

If this happens regularly, it may be worth paying attention to how they're breathing while they sleep.

settings.heading: You Notice Their Mouth Is Open While They Sleep
settings.subheading: This is one of the easiest signs to spot — once you know to look for it.
settings.body:
Check on them after they've been asleep for a little while.

Are their lips gently closed? Or is their mouth hanging open?

Many parents simply never think to check.

settings.heading: They Toss, Turn or Seem Restless
settings.subheading: Being in bed for 10 hours doesn't necessarily mean getting 10 hours of high-quality sleep.
settings.body: If your child frequently changes positions, kicks off the covers or seems unusually restless during the night, it may be worth looking at their overall sleep habits — including how they breathe.

settings.heading: They're Tired Even After a Full Night's Sleep
settings.body:
Sound familiar?

Sleep isn't just about quantity. Quality matters, too.

If mornings are consistently difficult or your child still seems exhausted after plenty of time in bed, their nighttime routine and sleep quality may deserve a closer look.

settings.heading: Mornings Come With Irritability or Crankiness
settings.body:
But when waking up tired, moody or irritable becomes the norm, parents may want to look beyond bedtime itself.

Sometimes the question isn't:
"How long did they sleep?"
It's:
"How well did they sleep?"

settings.heading: They Have Trouble Focusing During the Day
settings.subheading: Sleep and daytime behavior are closely connected.
settings.body:
When kids don't get restorative sleep, it can show up during the day as difficulty concentrating, low energy or simply seeming "off."

That doesn't automatically mean nighttime breathing is the cause — but sleep quality is an important piece of the puzzle.

settings.heading: You Hear Snoring or Noisy Breathing
settings.subheading: Children can occasionally snore, especially when they're congested.
settings.body:
But frequent snoring, loud breathing, gasping or noticeable difficulty breathing during sleep deserves attention.

If your child regularly snores, gasps, struggles to breathe or you suspect a sleep or airway issue, talk with their pediatrician, dentist or another qualified healthcare professional.

settings.text: You already think about their bedtime.
